utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to the interpreters, although I don't hear them yet, since I can't see them. All right. Good afternoon to Prosecution and Defence counsel, to the accused. Mr. Greaves, how do you feel? Do you feel better?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you had a good weekend? Mr. Jelisic, do you feel all right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [interpretation] Yes, I do, much better. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We can have the witness brought in, and I think that Mr. Greaves should finish the cross-examination of this witness. Mr. Registrar, have our witness brought in. Here he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated, Mr. Didic. This is a public hearing. Let me remind you that you are still under oath. I hope the weekend in The Hague was not too long for you. Did you have a good weekend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, everything is all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you able to visit the city a little bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If you've gotten your strength back, you can now continue to answer the questions that Mr. Greaves is going to ask you, Mr. Greaves, the defence counsel for Mr. Goran Jelisic. Mr. Greaves, please proceed. Did I make a mistake? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, I want to ask you now about the interrogations concerning which you gave evidence on Friday afternoon of last week. Firstly, can you help me, please, about this: When you were interrogated, in what topics were those who interrogated you interested?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: As I came from the area controlled by the army of BiH, I don't know what it was called then, the defence, they were asking me about its strength, about weapons, how many people were there, what was going on on the ground, who had a rifle, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: By the time you had been arrested, had you in any way taken part in military activities in that area?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Had you seen military activities about which you could talk?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Combat activities were conducted 15 kilometres from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So is it right, therefore, that you were unable in any way to answer the questions that you were being asked?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: It is, yes, because I knew nothing about the forces or the Green Berets or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Is that what you told them, that you knew nothing, or did you tell them anything that they wanted to hear?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I told them I knew nothing, but the interrogation and maltreatment went on. They beat me and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So they didn't accept that you knew nothing of what was going on. Did they give you a reason as to why they didn't accept that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know. They thought that I knew something, but I didn't. I was not involved in anything and I knew nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, I want now to ask you a little more detail about the interrogations that you say were conducted.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Well, the interrogation was -- how should I put it? Goran interrogated me two or three times, asking me who was armed, who had a rifle, what was going on up there, but I didn't know about that, and the rest was as usual. He would take me out, beat me with various objects, with batons, his feet, broke Coca-Cola bottles against my head, and things like that. That is the routine. The only thing he didn't like was that I was a Muslim; that is how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this right, Mr. Didic: that, in fact, the first interrogation that was conducted with you was on the 19th of May, not the 20th?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: The first day, the first day when I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. According to you, although this is not accepted by the Defence, according to you, you were arrested on the 19th and taken to Luka on the 19th. So what --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: On the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you is that the first interrogation conducted with you was on that day, the first day that you were at Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: By somebody called Dragisa Tesic or Dragan Tesic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know the names of people who took us. There were two of them in multicoloured uniforms. But I didn't know those people, so I cannot really say what their names were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, I suggest to you that it's not right that you didn't know who it was. You told the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when you gave them an account of these matters, you told them that you'd been interrogated not by two men in uniform but by a man called Dragisa Tesic and two men in uniform; in other words, three people in all, one of whom you did, in fact, know?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I may have seen them, but I didn't know any one of them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: By comparison, what you told the Office of the Prosecutor, in 1995, was that your first interrogation had been on 20th of May and that had been conducted by five people: two soldiers and three civilians. Do you remember telling the Office of the Prosecutor that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I remember saying that there were three of them when they interrogated me, but I do not know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What you were interrogated about were the activities of what was going on and what was described as the free territories?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the second interrogation that was conducted with you. Again, you told the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 that that had been on the 19th of May, not the 20th, and it was conducted by Kole.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: No. I don't think I stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, the -- would you like to have a copy, in Bosnian, of the original statement from which I'm working, that purports to have been made by you? Would that assist you to refresh your memory, Mr. Didic? I don't want to be unkind to you if you don't think you said that. Would that help you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not have an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Didic, did you understand the question that Mr. Greaves asked you? Do you want the question repeated?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Will you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, I'm not wanting to take advantage in any way of you and your memory. Do you recall making two statements about matters concerning your detention in Luka, one in 1992 to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities; that is, the District Court at Tuzla? Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: When I came out I did give a statement in 1992, and then I gave no more statements until the end of the war; that is, when people from The Hague Tribunal came.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So made a second statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1995. Would it assist you in answering the question that I've asked about the second interrogation, and that having been conducted by Kole, would it assist you to see the statement that you made to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities so that you can refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can have a look at the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got a copy in the Bosnian version. It has some underlinings in it. I don't know whether my learned friend has a clean copy or whether he objects to my showing him one with some underlinings. I don't suppose the witness will understand the underlinings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the usher please come and assist me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, I'd like you to look at that document, please. First of all, would you just help me by looking at each of the four pages that you've got there? Does your signature appear on each page?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: It does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you recall that that was the document which was produced for the District Court at Tuzla, by you, in association with those who were interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I gave that statement in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like you to look, please -- it may be on the second page. My version is in English, so the pages will be slightly different, Mr. Didic. Could you look, first of all, for a paragraph which I think starts: "After I told them everything"? Yes. It may be in the English version it's been translated slightly different, I'm told. It reads like this, so you can find it: "After I told them everything, they sent me back to the hangar, and some 20 to 30 minutes later we were taken out again one by one." Can you see that phrase or something similar to that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's this first sentence here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Could you just read that entire section down to: "From time to time we would hear singing and gunshots to the air"? Just a couple of sentences more.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: "When we told them all, they took us back to the hangar some 20 or 30 minutes. They again took us out one by one for interrogation. In the same building and in another office, we were interrogated by Kole. He was alone. "After the interrogation we were taken back to the hangar, and there we spent the night on the concrete in the part of the hangar where there were about 100 inmates. From that part we could hear singing."

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Didic. That's all I need for the moment. Do you see there that what you are saying to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities is that you were interviewed by the man Kole but made no mention at all about being interviewed by Goran Jelisic, Monika, and on that occasion Dragan Tesic? Do you understand that there is a difference between those two things?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: It is quite possible there is a difference, but I gave that statement and then after the war I again gave this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you were interviewed by the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- I'm sorry, my learned friend has an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like the Defence, when the Defence refers to prior witness statements, to refer exactly to what is in the statement. For instance, the Defence referred to this statement, that the witness never -- that the witness said that he had been interrogated on May 19. If you look at the Bosnian government statement, he never said that. He said on May 19 he was taken to the camp but never mentioned that he was interviewed on May 19. The same with this last question. When the witness was asked why he didn't mention that Goran was at the interrogation, it is on page 2 of his Bosnia statement where he says: "I saw Dragan Zivkovic, Goran Jelisic, and Monika, who was short," and so on. "As soon as I stepped outside, they started to beat me." So he mentioned that Goran was there, that Goran beat him. So I would like the Defence to refer exactly to what the witness said in his statement to the Bosnian government. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: With great respect to my learned friend, I'm doing exactly that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The objection is sustained. Mr. Greaves, if you quote something, you must quote the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, I'm just about to tell you that my learned friend is not correct in what he says. I really don't want to get bogged down in this, but I'm looking at the statement. He says, quite clearly, arrested on May the 19th. He then gives an account of what happened to him on May the 19th, and after the passage which has just been read out, after, he says this: "In the evening the next day, about 2100 hours on May the 20th." Unless I have missed something, the passage before that clearly refers to the 19th of May. I'm therefore asking about two interrogations and, in fact, third, which this witness said to Bosnia-Herzegovina happened on the 19th of May. If there is a dispute that my reading of that statement is incorrect, then of course I'm sure my learned friend will put that to me, but unless the words: "In the evening the next day, about 2100 hours on May the 20th," means something completely different, then what I'm asking about is the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Greaves. I would like to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to turn to the Prosecution and to the Defence and say that the Judges would like, on the basis of Rule 98, that whenever there is a contradiction shown by the Defence or the Prosecution, that is, between the statements made before the Tuzla Tribunal, I'm not sure why it was a court, whereas one talks about the Tribunal at Tuzla and other times the government, but let me go back to my major problem. The Defence, and let me turn to Mr. Didic, has the basic right to try to find out whether there were any contradictions in your statement and to put your credibility in question. I'm sure that you will explain that these are the legal and judicial subtleties that are very important for the accused. As for the Judges, they have just deliberated and consider that whenever there is an alleged contradiction that the Defence wants to show between the statements made by a witness before the Tribunal at Tuzla, that is, Witness X, and the statements made to the Office of the Prosecutor, the Judges would like that an exhibit be tendered for these debates that will also apply to the previous witness once those statements indicate that they are from the Tribunal at Tuzla, because the Judges are sensitive to the fact that contradictions are being shown between the various statements of the witnesses, but these statements were given at different times, frequently in different contexts, and the Judges are very mindful of the need for consistency in these statements because, obviously, over hours and hours of statements there may be, and there certainly must be contradictions, some of which apparently are very important. I'm not speaking specifically of you, Mr. Didic. This has happened with witnesses that preceded you as well. Therefore, I wanted to indicate the decision of the Judges; that is, that in the three languages the statements be provided -- I don't know who has them -- made before the Tribunal at Tuzla, which will allow the Judges to evaluate the consistency of all the statements and to reach an idea as to the specific credibility of the witness. You may now continue, Mr. Greaves, unless there are any questions that you wish to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. It's a practical one. As far as I know, these statements exist in their original form; in other words, in the form of the B/C/S language group, and I have a copy in English. I don't know in what language Your Honour would prefer to have these submitted to you, but I'm only in a position to give you a copy in English, and I don't know whether you would prefer to have it in French. I say that's a practical issue, because the Defence has absolutely no funds or facilities for having things translated into French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the Office of the Prosecutor has its own version. I think the best thing for us would be to have the B/C/S version -- to have it translated. Mr. Tochilovsky, do you have those statements that were given in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have all these statements. We'll check if they were translated into French. If not, we'll send for translation into French those statements which were already admitted into exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At the end of the proceedings we will assign a number. Registrar, we won't use numbers now, but once the Prosecution has completed its case we will see the reference numbers we need for the various exhibits, and we can say this was the Tribunal's exhibit because it is the Tribunal which was requesting them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. It will be indicated as is done in other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. You may now proceed, Mr. Greaves. Let me remind you that you must continue to try to prove that the Prosecutor's assumption of genocide, thesis of genocide, is not correct, and I would like you to keep that firmly in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry to harp on about the practicalities. I just want to know what, (A), I'm allowed to do with this witness; and, (B), whether you need, for immediate use, a copy in English of what's presently available, because Your Honour hasn't indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, no. Not at all. It's just pursuant to Rule 98, the Judges have exhibits tendered, have them numbered, and the number -- the version that will be translated into French is supplied by the Office of the Prosecutor. It will be translated into French. So for the time being you have nothing further to do, but you should be informed. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the other thing that Your Honour didn't tell me was can I continue on the assumption that what I have read out is a correct reading of the statement? Your Honour didn't indicate that. Otherwise, it's going to make it very difficult for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we don't have it in front of us, and the Judges will decide in due course. I don't have the statement. Mr. Tochilovsky says that you did not fully read the quotation. It sort of went out in the air like that. It's a bit more complicated for me. I think the best thing would be for you to continue with what you've done, and we will rule when our minds are clear. Perhaps both of you are right. Perhaps you are reading passages which different people would interpret differently. That's all I can tell you right now. However, I do commit you to remain within the scope of the examination in chief and not to lose sight of the fact that your only right is to refute the charge of genocide and never to forget that Goran Jelisic acknowledged the counts and that he pleaded guilty to those counts which inter alia concern this witness. Mr. Tochilovsky, do you want to intervene again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just on the same issue. Since we are going to send translation, interpretation of those Bosnian statements which the Defence use as the exhibits, my understanding is that the Judges accepted that both the Bosnian statement and the statement taken by the Office of the Prosecutor are to be submitted together as exhibits. In this case, both of them are to be submitted to the French translation and it will take some time. So we disclosed to the Defence those statements in English because it was our obligation under Rule 66. Now we'll submit them for French translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but during this time I'd ask the registrar that as soon as they have been provided in English that they be translated immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this holds only when the Defence points out a contradiction in his statements as compared with the statements made before the Tribunal at Tuzla. We're not doing it for all witnesses, but only for two where Mr. Greaves has pointed out a number of contradictions. In other words, with these statements which must expressly be attached to the case file, the Judges wanted to examine the total consistency of the statements to see what is the witness's credibility. Mr. Didic, do not lose your concentration. This is a judicial argument, which is natural in a tribunal, but you've understood the essential point; that is, the Defence wants to bring out the contradictions in your various statements. The Prosecutor, who has called you as a witness, considers that the contradictions were not properly quoted by the Defence, and so the Judges are saying, "Give us the statements and we will make our own evaluation." Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Greaves, you may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, I don't know how much you've followed of that argument, but let me just take you back to where we were. You had just read a short portion of your statement made to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities, and I was putting to you that, in reference to that interview that you related there, you were interviewed only by Kole, and not by two soldiers and three -- I'm sorry, by Goran Jelisic, Monika, Kole, and Dragan Tesic. Can you help me about this: The matters which you recounted in 1992, were they fresh in your mind at the time?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I made that statement three months after my exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So is the effect of what you said, "Yes, they were, indeed, fresh in my mind"? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If you need to look at your statement again, please do so and please indicate that you would like to do so. You said also, and I suggest this relates to the 19th of May, that you were interrogated a third time by three men whom you did not know on that occasion, after which you were put into a different part of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: That was on the 20th of May, not the 19th. I was transferred to the other part of the hangar where there was a sliding door.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is it right that some people were released at about that time, Mr. Didic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anybody being released.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was one of them the manager of Agro Banka, a grey-haired elderly man, a man whose first name was Amir, a large black-haired corpulent man? Does that help you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: All of us who were brought from the SUP were there, and then those who were interrogated went to the other hangar. It's not that we were all interrogated at the same time; we went out one by one to the office, and then those who had been interrogated were taken to the other part of the hangar where the other inmates were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you now, please, about this: Is it right that as well as the name "Adolf" being applied to Goran Jelisic, you also heard him being referred to as, I think the word is, "Duke" or "Vojvoda"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Right. His friends addressed him that way. I did not know Goran or Vojvoda. That's how they referred to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As far as Goran Jelisic saying that he had killed people at the Sava River, again, I suggest you made no mention of that in your statement to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities and that's something that you've made up since that time, Mr. Didic.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not make anything up. You cannot give a detailed account of each and every hour that was spent there and every single word that was uttered, but I was there, I experienced all of that, and I know what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this right, Mr. Didic: that as far as you were concerned, the commander of the camp, whilst you were there, was the man called Kole?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you know that person's second name or did you come to learn it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Everybody called him Kole. I knew his first and last name, but I forgot them. But I know he and Monika were brother and sister or half-brother and half-sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If I said the name "Kosta Simonovic", would that refresh your memory as to who he was?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was no audible answer from the witness. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, I think I heard what you said, but could you please repeat your answer so that the interpreters can hear? I think they missed it.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Kole's name sounds familiar to me now that I've heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So that Their Honours, when they have in front of them the statements they've been asking for, should know the circumstances, when you gave your account to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities -- and I'd like you to look, please, at the last paragraph of your statement, if you'd be so kind, Mr. Didic -- when you signed it, did the final paragraph have this: "At the end, I state that the full text of this statement was read to me, after having been formulated with my participation. I'm ready to repeat everything I stated here in court or before some international commission which might be interested in the matter." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just so we can have this clear, was it, in fact, read over to you before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And when it says "... having been formulated with my participation," did you dictate it or was it put into words by those who were asking the questions?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Some people put questions to me and I answered them, and that was put down and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can I just hear this answer again? He said, "Some people put questions to me and I answered them, and that was put down ..." Your question, in fact, was who put it down?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let me just look again at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Your question was: "... was it put into words by those who were asking the questions?"

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I asked him an alternative question. I asked him if he dictated it or was it put into words by those who were asking the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, his answer is not clear, for the second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. I took it that he had clarified what I'd asked him, and his answer was, "I was asked questions, I answered them, and it was the answers which were put down" but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not in his words, because you asked, was it put down in his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let me clarify it with him, if I may, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, does it come to this: that you were asked questions by those who were writing out the statement, you gave the answers, and it was your answers which were written down and which you then subsequently signed as being correct? Is that a fair summary of what happened when you made that statement?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I hope this assists in answering Your Honour's question, and I hope that I made it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Didic. Mr. Didic, I'm coming close to the end. If I may, I want to ask you about the time when you were transferred, which I think was sometime in July. Is it right that at that time, everybody at Luka was transferred out of the facility?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I think that everybody was transferred to Batkovici. There were eight or nine buses. We were all transferred. I don't know if anyone stayed back. I don't think anyone remained. I don't know whether they brought in some other people afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is this right: that when you were transferred, by that time, there were something like 450 detainees at Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, 400, 450. I wouldn't know the exact number, but that's the number approximately that was transferred from Luka to Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In the period when you were at Luka, would this be right: that the population had changed in the sense that people had been released, new people had come in, and that that was a constant process throughout your stay at Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Before people from Brezovo Polje were brought in, the situation was always, approximately, more or less the same, 90 to 100 people, I don't know exactly, until they brought in these people from Brezovo Polje. From Brezovo Polje, they brought in about 350 persons. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The people that you've described as coming or being there before the arrivals from Brezovo Polje, that 90 to 100 people, was that the same 90 to 100 people that remained a constant group?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The people who arrived from Brezovo Polje, were they -- I'm sorry. Let me start again. The people in the group before the arrivals from Brezovo Polje, were they of all ages and sexes or restricted to men between the ages of 18 and 60 or 18 and 65?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Men. They were men from 18 to 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In relation to the group that was transferred from Brezovo Polje, is that limitation the same for them? Were they men between the age of 18 and 60/65?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: There were younger ones too, children too. There were children who were not even 18 yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you say "children," are you saying small children or just young men who were teenagers?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to teenagers. I'm not referring to very young children, but I'm just saying that they weren't even 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems that the word "teenager" is a universal word, Mr. Didic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just give me a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you just give us a date when the people from Brezovo Polje were brought in? Would that be around June?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact date. They were brought in in June, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were they put into the second hangar?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Again -- oh, I see the answer has come up on the transcript. Mr. Didic, I want to conclude, please, by asking you this: You were able to say that you'd heard of two of the people on the lists, Novalic and Osman Vatic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There were two lists, were there, that you were taken through, one long one and one slightly shorter?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I recognised those two names on those lists; that's it: Novalic and Osman Vatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And Amir Novalic, you heard that he'd been killed at the SUP building. From whom did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I heard about it from a man whom they brought in to Luka, but he was killed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is that the only information you were told? Were you told when he was killed or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: I do not know the exact date, but I heard that story, that Amir Novalic was killed in SUP. I don't know who killed him, though. I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As far as Osman Vatic was concerned, is this right: He was at Batkovici with you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was in the Luka camp, and then we were transferred together to Batkovici and then taken home, but we heard subsequently that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was he released before you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you remind us of the date when you left? I think it was October the 5th, is that right, when you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We could not hear the answer. We're sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, you're dropping your voice. I know it's not very easy, and we're very, very close to the end. Can you just repeat your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of October, 1992, that is when I was exchanged at Dornji Rahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How long before you were exchanged would you say that Osman Vatic left Batkovici camp?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Could have been a month and a half or two. I wouldn't know the date because there were too many of us there. I don't think anyone could remember the exact date, but I know that he left quite a long time before I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Didic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Greaves. Mr. Tochilovsky, please proceed. Do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Judge Riad? Judge Rodrigues? No questions. I have no questions. Thank you, Mr. Didic. It wasn't too long, but you did have to spend the weekend here. Thank you very much for coming to The Hague. On behalf of my colleagues, we wish you good luck in the rest of your life, and we hope that you can try to forget these tragic events. We are now going to take care of you. Perhaps you need a few more moments to prepare the next witness. The afternoon is going to be long, so perhaps we should take a 15-minute break. All right. We will take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness H, please remain standing for a few moments. We're going to call you Witness H because the Tribunal has granted you all the protective measures that you've asked for. We're going to ask you to take an oath that the usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. You have agreed that the name that was shown you is, in fact, your name; is that correct? Don't say it, though; just look at it. Do not say what you see; simply say "Yes" if it is, in fact, your name. Thank you. Thank you for having come --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to the International Tribunal as part of the trial here of Goran Jelisic, who is in the accused's box on your left. First you will answer questions that the Prosecutor asks you. I'm sure this was explained to you. After that you will be asked questions by Defence counsel. Mr. Prosecutor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I have the usher's assistance in placing the summary of the witness's statements in front of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness H, is this the summary of your statements that you had the opportunity to read?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Is this a correct summary of your statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness H, before the war did you live in Mujkici in Brcko, before the war started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Were you admitted to a local hospital on May 4, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Were you then taken to Luka camp from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: And what is the date? When were you taken to Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: The 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Where were you kept when you were in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: The first hangar, the hangar which served for interrogations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was a man by the name Muhamed Bukvic in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: There was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: How was the man treated in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: When I saw him, I couldn't recognise him, because he was so badly beaten that his head was unrecognisable. He approached me and told me that he was so-and-so, and he also said who it was who beat him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Who beat him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: According to him, he was mostly beaten by Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did he tell you why Jelisic beat him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: As one needed no reason to hit a man, we did not discuss reasons, because it often happened even without knowing who was coming that that person would be beaten; that is, one simply did not ask why and why he had been brought to Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Was a man by the name Kolar or Alija in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you know who brought him to Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: He was brought by two soldiers escorting Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Jelisic accuse Alija of anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: He did. That man, I think he was in his 70s, and his hand -- one of his hands, I don't remember whether left or right, was bandaged. He (sic) said that he was a sniper and that he'd been caught somewhere beating Serb troops. I believe that the man was old enough not to be able to pick up a rifle, that is, to look through the sights, let alone be a sniper at that advanced age.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did that 70-year-old tell you how he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No. We did not talk much, as he really was not up to it. When he -- he was beaten severely when he came back to the hangar, and he could not talk much, but he said that they found him somewhere in the street, and that was all that we learned from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did you see who beat Alija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know who beat him before that, before he was brought into the hangar, but I do know, since Alija was sitting next to me, that Mr. Jelisic -- and I don't know where he got that particular tool, it was a short metal shovel with a wooden handle, and he hit him a couple of times. I repeat, I did not see, before he entered, whether he had been beaten or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Was Alija then brought back to the hangar after he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Alija was lying down next to us; rather, next to me, next to Bukvic; there were two or three detainees more there -- I remember a name. I don't remember other names -- for awhile. I can't remember whether it was an hour, an hour and a half, Alija, again escorted by two uniformed men, was taken out from the hangar; and across the hangar was Mr. Jelisic, and I don't know whether it was deliberately or by accident, met him and hit him a couple of times with a metal rod. I suppose -- I guess that it was a rod with which you open a manhole or something for water supply. Mr. Jelisic had a car parked there; rather, he had come in a car. So he entered the car and left with Monika, in the direction of the petrol station. A few minutes later, the old gentleman was brought into the hangar by two soldiers. I remember both of them. One had yellow hair. We learnt later that he came from Trnova, in the municipality of Bijeljina, and just deposited him in the same place from which they had taken him away. The man was all battered and could not move. He gave no sign of life and he was already beginning to moan. I had a piece of cardboard with me. We were all sitting down on a cardboard. I tried to somehow push it under his head, but he issued a death throe and died. May I mention that after a certain time Mr. Jelisic drove in with his car, into the hangar, and there he ordered a soldier, and there were two of them, to bring some water, a bucket of water. That soldier who brought the bucket with water threw it over Alija's body, but since the death must have occurred before that, the fact that the water was poured over him did not change anything. The man did not move. But Mr. Jelisic then said, "Old body -- old heart and could not endure."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. H. Was a man, Stjepan Itric, detained in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Who brought this man to the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I don't know who brought him to the hangar, but it was Jelisic who brought him into the hangar. I know Stjepan Itric personally, as we were next-door neighbours. I think we've known one another for 30 years or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Mr. H, did Jelisic accuse Itric of anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. As he was brought into the hangar, Mr. Itric was beaten on the head. Naturally, I do not know about other parts of the body because we could not see them. But Jelisic, as they came into the hangar, told Mr. Itric to sit down on a chair in the left corner, from which nobody had got up yet, and accused him of having raped a 7-year-old Serb child.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Witness H, when you answer the questions, please turn to the Judges. Thank you. You may continue, Mr. Tochilovsky.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness H, you mentioned that you knew Stjepan Itric before the war. Can you characterise the man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him personally. At that time, he could have been about 40 or so, and I really doubt whether he was guilty of what he was being accused of. Knowing the man, he was a man who we never saw with a woman, let alone doing what they were charging him with. He was a very withdrawn person. Meanwhile, after Mr. Jelisic went out, I was not far from Itric, so I went to him and asked him about the circumstances that he had been brought there. He began to explain, we were whispering or talking very softly, and he said that he'd gone out to buy cigarettes for his father, and he had crossed the railway tracks, it was about 500 metres from his home, and that that is where he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Was Stjepan Itric beaten in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes, he was rather badly beaten, battered. I believe there was a soldier called Dragan, I think, in a multicoloured uniform, and he would come with another soldier. I can't remember how many times they came that night. They would take him out, but he always said -- naturally, as much as one could talk -- that he was always in Mr. Jelisic's office and that all the beatings that he got, according to him, came from that particular gentleman. But there was also side beatings as well by those soldiers who would take him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you know the fate of this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I do, unfortunately. He was taken away one night, I believe it was the second night, and we heard screams and cries that he was not guilty of what he was being charged with. But Itric is no longer among the living, and we do not know the circumstances, whether he died due to the injuries he received or whether he was shot dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness H, he was a wall painter from the hospital in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, there were two house painters. One was killed before. I don't know who. The other house painter was with us and he was distributing the food, the food, I mean, which we got there in Luka. That evening, after the evening meal -- I couldn't remember what time it was -- a soldier came and asked for the person who had distributed milk that evening. May I mention that that evening, we were issued milk and cornmeal. I remember that very well. I just happened to be next to a pile of socks, I was looking for a pair of socks for myself, and I saw Mr. Jelisic outside by the door. The gentleman who had been called out went out, and one could hear only two blunt shots. I could not see who killed him, whether it was Mr. Jelisic, from his pistol which he always carried, or somebody else, but we did see the dead body on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Was there any particular sound? Did you recognise the shot when the person was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: It was the first time I heard a sound like that, but those who had been in Luka for some time already told me that that was the usual sound of a Scorpio with a silencer. But I'd never even seen that pistol before, nor had I heard a shot fired from it. This is what other detainees told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Were you interrogated by Dragisa Tesic in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Tesic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did Tesic tell you anything about your release from Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. As I entered Mr. Tesic's and Kavrinovic's office, Mr. Tesic, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: (redacted), he came out and told me not to worry, that he would rescue me but that he would have to consult Mr. Jelisic about it, after all. I didn't know what particular duties they performed, but I realised, from what Mr. Tesic had told me, that the commander of Luka -- that is how I saw it -- was Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Was there an announcement in Luka that there would be no further killings in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I must apologise first if I go wrong with the dates. It's quite possible because, after all, seven years have elapsed since then. But I believe it was around the 16th of May that Mr. Jelisic came and said that there would be no more killings at Luka. Nonetheless, there was yet another case of somebody being taken away, and that was Suljo Pezerovic. He was wearing pyjamas because he had been brought from the hospital, and unfortunately he is no longer among the living.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Was there a detainee by the name of Ohro in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ohro Ozegovic was with us at Luka. I don't know when he came. But one evening, Mr. Ozegovic left the hangar and, after a certain period of time, came back in a customs officer's uniform with a baton in his hand, escorted by Mr. Jelisic. Presumably, he must have been given instructions as to what to do to the rest of us detainees or prisoners. I heard with my own ears, and all the other detainees did, Mr. Jelisic say, "Mind you, don't you try and say anything to Mr. Ozegovic." It was a frequent scene. Mr. Ozegovic would go out to Mr. Jelisic, and there he would give him a drink or offer him a certain dose of alcohol, I don't know the quantity, and then he would come back to the hangar, beat us. I myself was beaten one night by Mr. Ozegovic. That evening, Mr. Jelisic entered in a vehicle with his lights on, stopped, and we, that is, all the detainees, had to pass in front of those car lights. I don't know whom he was looking for, but Mr. Ozegovic battered quite a number of our Bosniak fellows, guys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness H, when were you released from Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I was released on the 27th of May, sometime in the morning, around 9.00, 10.00. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Were you then rearrested and detained in Batkovici camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Unfortunately, on the 13th of July, not only I, but everybody who happened to be in the locality of Es were taken to Batkovici. I believe there were two buses that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did you see Goran Jelisic when you were in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: In the latter half of September, I don't remember the date, somebody may have noted it down, but Goran Jelisic came to the camp at Batkovici. Why? Because he was looking for detainees from Luka who would testify, according to those who went in front of Novi Sad Television cameras, that Mr. Jelisic had not ill-treated or killed anyone at the Luka camp. Among the witnesses whom Mr. Jelisic was looking for was Mr. Ozegovic, who had been to Luka, and I already explained what he had been doing at Luka. So Fikret, called Pikric, also volunteered, and he had not been to Luka, and Pajzer, I don't know his name, from Zenica, who had not been to Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Now we will turn to the list of names you were shown prior to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to place in front of the witness Exhibit 12 and then Exhibit 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: First, Exhibit 12. On page 1, you can see the name Sakib Becirevic. Do you know the fate of this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I know he was killed, but I don't know where. His nickname is Kibe. He was a butcher. Yes, we knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: You didn't see the killing, but you heard about it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: On the 11th is when I came to Luka, and according to what I was told, he had been killed in the barracks, but I did not see it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: The next name on the page is Midhat Bukvic. What do you know about this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Midhat Bukvic could have been in his 40s or 40-odd. He was the brother of the Bukvic we mentioned who was so badly battered at Luka. He lived in my neighbourhood, (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: According to his brother, he was killed at Luka. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: On the same page, Stipo Glavosevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I think that all of those who were at Luka at the time knew Stipo. I have heard about him. I knew Stipo personally. Stipo perhaps lived 100 metres away from Mr. Midhat Bukvic. He was a lawyer by profession. According to detainees at Luka, his ears were cut off, and he was killed at Luka in the same hangar where I was taken to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Page 2 of the same exhibit. In the middle of the list, you can see the name Sadik Jukic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. We called him Sadan. He could have been born in 1932 or 1933. (redacted) (redacted). He was a pensioner. I am told that he was killed in Mujkici, (redacted), but I do not know who could be the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Next after Jukic is Jusuf Kapkovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Jusuf Kapkovic is a man who lived at Klanac, had his own house there. He had five or six children and I know them. I believe it was on the 16th of June that he left and never came back. We do not know where he went, but he's gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: On the same page, Kartal Rasim and Kartal Kasim, what do you know about these two men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Two brothers, Kasim and Rasim Kartal. Rasim Kartal's wife worked at the same place where I worked. I know both of them very well. They were athletes. They were sportsmen in Brcko. According to people who stayed at Luka, they were killed on the same day at Luka, but I must mention that I was not at Luka at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: On the same page, Sadik Kombic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Sadik Kombic lived in Novo Brcko. His family's still in Rahic, as his are in Donja Rahic. He lived near my mother's. I knew him since childhood. I believe we're almost of the same age. There may be a year or two of difference. He disappeared and I do not know who killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Next page, page 3. The middle of the list you can see a name, Muranjkovic Galib.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I think that about 70 per cent of Brcko inhabitants knew Galib Muranjkovic, because he was a very prominent citizen of Brcko. However, according to his son, who was detained at Batkovici, and I can't remember the date, he was taken from Janja, and there all trace of him is lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: On the same page, Pezerovic, Ibrahim; and Pezerovic, Sefko. What do you know about these two names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Two brothers. One, Ibrahim, worked the same place as I did, and Sefko was with the railways company. Around the 15th or 16th of May they left home through Rijeka, and there our people, I mean our men from security, stopped them. They went home to collect some of their effects, but they do not seem to have either taken their effects or ever come back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Pezerovic Suljo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I've already mentioned, when describing Luka, I've already mentioned Suljo Residovic [Error in realtime]. He was a man who was brought from the hospital because he was wounded somewhere. He was a driver. I don't know the company he worked for, but he arrived there in blue pyjamas. He arrived at Luka wearing blue pyjamas. After the 15th or 16th, I cannot recall the date, he was taken away and never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: On the same page --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think the transcript has used a different name for the surname of the man that this witness mentioned. I think it's incorrect. Can my learned friend indicate that he was asking about Suljo Pezerovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Suljo Pezerovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: The next name is Pobric Senad.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Senad Pobric, Sefko Pezerovic, Brahim Pezerovic, they're all of my mother's neighbours. Senad was a child -- I don't mean child really, but much younger than I am. He disappeared early in May. Where and how, I don't know, but I know his mother. His mother lives in the area of Rahic, that is area of Palanka, with a daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: The last page of this document, the name Vugrincic Franjo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. A man who lived at Meraje. He was a repair mechanic for electrical appliances. He was taken away from Marija. When, I don't know, but he does not be among the living any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Let me turn to Exhibit 13 now. At number 2 there is the name Ahmet Hodzic. What do you know about this man? What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: A man who was highly regarded by all. At that time he also had a thriving business. He lived in a part of Brcko called Mujkici. We call it that way. When he was killed, I do not know, but according to the stories of those who were detained in the mosque, he was taken away and never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Number 3, there is the name Husein Kaknjo. What do you know about his fate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I know Husein Kaknjo very well, since I bought a plot of land in Mujkici from that gentleman to build a house of my own. I heard that he remained there in Brcko, that he's no longer among the living, but I'm telling you that at I think he was well over 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: He's not among the living. Nobody talks about him. I go to Brcko very seldom, but I heard that he was taken away because they claimed that he was -- he was a man who made major contributions, lots of money, to the SDA party. At any rate, he's no longer among the living.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Numbers 6 and 7, there are names of Kasim Kartal and Rasim Kartal. What do you know about those two men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I think that in my previous statement I said that Kasim and Rasim were two brothers and that they were killed in Luka. You have my statement from Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Number 16, there is the name Sakib Becirevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. That's Kibe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: So this is the Kibe you gave testimony about today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, yes, yes. That's the man. We all called him Kibe. I didn't even know that Sakib was his real name. He was a butcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Number 17, Sakib Edhemovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Sakib Edhemovic. One of the best surgeons in the canton of Tuzla. We all knew him as a physician. During the war he stayed in Brcko. They say that he was killed in Brcko. I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Number 23, Vasif Sulejmanovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Vasif Sulejmanovic had a private business. He owned a TV station in Brcko. Vasif remained in Brcko. They say that he was often seen in Brcko with a white armband of some kind, but afterwards he was not seen. What happened to him, that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: And number 27, there is the name Muhamed Zelenjakovic. What do you know about this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Muhamed Zelenjakovic worked at the hospital as a barber. I know him personally. I know him well. I know all three brothers well. All three were barbers. Two of them had barber shops of their own and he was employed in the hospital. But he remained there with his son. He is no longer among the living. His son is no longer among the living.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Number 33, Himzo Kevric. Do you know what happened to this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Himzo Kevric was in charge of the Novi Dom shop across the street from the bank. All of us in Brcko know him. Well, not everybody, but 90 per cent of us at least. All adults know him. He retired just before the war. He stayed in his own home, the one that he had in the Serb part of town, together with Mr. Sejdalija Muminovic. People say -- I heard this -- he was killed on the 16th of June, in his basement. I wish to mention that I was not there and I could not go there at the time, but I heard that story. At any rate, both gentlemen are no longer among the living.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: You've just mentioned Sejdalija Muminovic. Is that the name under 34?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Number 36, Osman Vatic. Do you know the fate of this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I don't know. I would kindly ask the Court to allow me to go back to Luka once again as far as Osman Vatic is concerned. Osman Vatic is a respectable lawyer in Brcko. He was highly respected by all. He was brought into Luka. He was put on a chair. As I say, I cannot remember the date. Mr. Jelisic walked in after him and said, "This is man who gave 50.000 marks for the SDA party so that it could arm itself in order to kill the Serbs." I personally saw Osman Vatic in Batkovici as well. He was relieved from Batkovici at the end of September. I cannot recall the date. He was killed in front of his own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Do you know who killed him? Do you know any details about that killing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: There were different stories going around, but I'm not well-informed and I cannot give any other information as to who killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. H.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tochilovsky. Witness H, as I've already told you, you will now be asked some questions by the Defence. Let me turn to you, Mr. Greaves. Do you also intend to call the credibility of this witness in doing your cross-examination in respect of inconsistencies with the previous statements that he gave?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm not going to go quite as far as that. I'm going to just ask him about his memory and his ability to remember dates and detail. So it's not quite the same line of cross-examination as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know about how much time you're going to need, about?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would think about 40 minutes, but I hope to keep it a bit shorter than that, but please don't grumble if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: (Inaudible)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is your initial approximation, which is less than the hour, I'm not going to take you literally. You know, we apply our rules here with a degree of flexibility. Please begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. H, I'm going to ask you some questions. Please will you help me in this way: If you do not understand the question that I ask you, please don't be shy; stop me, tell me you don't understand it, and I'll try and rephrase it so that it's a better asked question. All right. Do you agree to do that with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. H, we're now some seven years on from the events -- seven years plus on from the events of May 1992. Would this be fair: that in the intervening period, some of the detail of dates and places and so on may have become, in your own mind, mixed up and you may have made mistakes about them? Would that be fair? It would be understandable if that were the case.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That's possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The reason that I ask you that is that in evidence today, you've told us that you went to Luka detention facility on the 11th of May, but when you gave an account of this matter to the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you indicated to them it was the 13th of May. Is it possible that you were, in fact, mistaken and it may have been the later date that you went to Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No. I doubt that I made a statement to anyone saying that it was on the 13th. I know that it was a Monday when I went to the hospital on the 4th of May, and I know that it was a Monday, the 11th, when I came in Luka. I don't know who I gave that kind of a statement to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Nothing very much may turn on it, but it's just -- really just to see whether you may be incorrect as to how long you were in Luka.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking is because we have your statement that you made to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities and it says 13th of May, but you think the earlier date is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. On the 13th of May or, rather, when I got out, two or three days later they asked me, perhaps, but I wish to mention that never in any statement I made to any authorities or any investigators did I give such a statement. I remember exactly which date and which day it was when I was arrested or, rather, when I was taken out of hospital, because I was a patient. I was a sick man. I remember my release very well as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right. Mr. H, help me about this, please: When you first got to Luka camp, were you accompanied by others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you arrived there, what time of day was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: We came in the morning, sometime around 10.00, 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning. I can't remember. There were eight of us and a woman. All of us were sick persons, in pyjamas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you arrived at Luka, is this right: You were shown initially into the hangar where other people were being detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: By people being detained, who were already there before you, how many people were there before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: As far as I could see, perhaps three or four in that part when I got in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And you spent about a fortnight or a bit more than a fortnight in the facility. During that time, did the population, if I may call it that, in terms of numbers, change at the facility? In other words, did some people get released, and other people, were they brought in so that the numbers were ever-changing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This happened very often, that some people would be released and would go home -- I don't know whether they would be home or elsewhere -- and others would be brought in. I can even say to you that, regrettably, there were women with children that were brought in from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In general, Mr. H, is this right: that by far, the majority of prisoners, detainees, were men, whether fit or unfit, like yourself, as it were, but men between the ages of 18 and 60 or 18 and 65? Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: The majority, yes, but I wish to mention to you that there were also men over 70 and even women. I told you a minute ago that there were even women with children there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, and I was just going to come to them. Is this also right, Mr. H: that some people came and were detained only for a very short period, sometimes came in and went out the same day or were released within two or three days, and others were kept for longer periods; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Certainly, yes, there were men who came together with me from the hospital. There was a man named Mujo. I can't remember his last name. He was released on the same day. Very often in the morning, they would call out a few names and release these persons, and there were some people who were released within the scope of an hour during the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the women and children whom you've described, in general, were they released almost immediately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I remember a family or, rather, two families, it's the Ramovic family, where all the family members, women and children included, I think they were with us for six or seven days. We all slept together. The other women, I think, came after the 16th of June. They were at the entrance into the hangar on the right-hand side. One was from Mujkici, Mirsada, and they were released after a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Help us about this, please: In the period of your detention at Luka, can you describe, on average, how many people were detained on any one day at the facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: A few minutes ago, we said that it was very difficult to tell because the number of people varied, and it is difficult to tell. I can say that the hangar, the one on the right-hand side, was full. We never counted the people who were there. We counted those who left and never returned, and where they went to, that, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like now to turn to this, please: Were you interrogated at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: On how many occasions were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you tell me this, please, Mr. H: Before the war began in May 1992, had you taken any part yourself in political life in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I was never interested in politics. I had a very good job in a work organisation where I worked quite a bit, and I was never active as far as political parties are concerned. Before that, I was in the former League of Communists or party, but I was only a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just so that we can be clear about this, would this be a fair comment, and if it's not, tell me immediately: Membership in the League of Communists was sometimes helpful in terms of one's career prospects. It didn't necessarily mean a strong attachment to the ideals of the party.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Since I did already have a career, I did not need political structures of the party in order to make a career for myself. I already had a career.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right, Mr. H.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please face the Judges when you give your answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. H, when you were interrogated, who was it who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Once I was interrogated by Mr. Tesic, but the first time, I was interrogated by some man called Sasa, as I later found out. I don't know where he was from, but I know that all the things I had -- and I'm probably not the only one to say this -- all the things I had that were any good, of any value, money, my watch, wallet, whatever, I had to leave with Mr. Sasa for safekeeping, and we know what kind of safekeeping that is. The other time, I was interrogated by Mr. Tesic, and that is all as far as interrogation is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Tesic, was he the person who interrogated you on the second interrogation or the first one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: The second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: On the first interrogation, apart from an interest in your valuables and so on, what else was the subject of that interrogation, Mr. H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: The subject was my arrival, my pre-war occupation. Another subject was who was rich in Brcko, who had lots of money, and a subject was how to reach these people. This gentleman, Sasa -- I don't know whether this is his name or nickname -- took the money of those people whom he interrogated, but he also wanted all these people to give their money to him of their own free will. I had a bit of trouble, unfortunately, because he blackmailed me. He said that by the next day, by 14.00, I should bring him 2.500 marks. If I didn't do so, he would kill me. However, I was fortunate enough, or perhaps to the regret of the others, he came the next day -- I don't know whether he came because of me or because of some other person, I don't know , but at any rate, he took away a prisoner who never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As far as your second interrogation was concerned, that was conducted by a police inspector, Mr. Tesic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. These were probably regular interrogations. I did not consult the other persons who were interrogated. (redacted) (redacted). Even while he was interrogating me and as he was going out into the hall, he mentioned to me in passing where my family was. This same Mr. Tesic, on the 27th of May, probably with the acquiescence of the commander of the camp, or whatever he was called, gave me a document stating that I could leave Luka. I have this document until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Apart from the issue of your release, was he asking about people who were involved in the SDA, people who were involved in military activities, people who were in the army, topics of that sort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was there an occasion when you were asked about your family, particularly with a view to finding out whether any of your family were in the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. He asked me how many children did I have; (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've just told us that you were given a pass and that you still have that document. Whereabouts is that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I can show it to you, if you like. Here it is. I can make a present of it also because it's a copy. I don't need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I wonder if I might have a look, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
