utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tochilovsky, this is a Prosecution witness. What is your opinion? We are discussing a document independently of what the Judges can see. What is your opinion about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before giving an opinion about the attachment of this document as an exhibit, we would like to see it first, if the Defence requests it as an attachment, but we don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Perhaps I can just go quickly to the heart of it. Perhaps I can have a look at it. If there's anything I want to ask about it, then I will proffer it and we'll see whether we need to have it. It may be that nothing turns on it at all. Would that be a sensible way to deal with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: We have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might see the document. Your Honours, give me a moment, please. Perhaps it could be shown to my learned friend for the Prosecution and then to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I don't know what this document concerns. It's in Serbo-Croat, I assume. Perhaps this could be given to the interpreters so that a side translation can be provided, and after that, we will admit it as an exhibit. For the continuation of these proceedings, it might be best first to have the translation of it. My colleague suggests that we put it on the ELMO --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think that that wouldn't be a good idea because it contains the name of the protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is the name, and the interpreters are also telling me that somebody has to read it out loud. All right. Can the interpreters interpret it or translate it, so long as the name is covered up? All right. Please try to work under those conditions. I think that would be the simplest way of proceeding; that is, we will put it on the ELMO but cover up the witness's name. But let's be sure that the copy is large enough so that the interpreters can work properly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It should be read out by somebody so that both booths can keep the pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was going to ask if the witness could read the details of the pass, excluding his own name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness H, can you see the screen properly and are you able to read the pass on that screen? I wonder whether you would be kind enough to go through each line and tell us what it says, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I don't have to read the first line because there is my name there. In the second line, it has the number of my identity card. After that, for a limited movement, for free movement between 6.00 until 21.00 in the combat area in the territory of the municipality of Brcko. The pass is valid only with the identity card, and signed "Serb Public Security Station," a signature, I don't know whose. But I should like to tell you something in relation to this document. I, and probably other detainees; that is, those who had their identity cards or driver's licenses or any kind of a personal document, were taken away, those documents, at Luka. I don't know where they were. So this document, it says that you must also show your identity card to have this pass valid, and yet there have been a number of cases, it also happened to my wife, where they simply tore up this kind of pass. Because there are all sorts of people there, so that I was not allowed to move about either. I'm telling you that I simply did not leave my flat until I was taken away to Batkovici. I never left my flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness H, could I just draw your attention, please, above your name, there are five lines of script at the top of the page. Could you also tell us what those say, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. "Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, SAO, Sambija, at Majrica, municipality of Brcko," the number of the document, "301/92, Brcko," dated the 27th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was that document signed in your presence or was it already signed when it was given to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: It was given to me personally, to my hands, but I don't know who signed it and I really cannot say who that is. I know where I was issued it, in Mr. Tesic's office, but whose signature this is, I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Although you didn't have your identity card, did you try and use this pass, and was it, on occasions, accepted as genuine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I already mentioned it before, that as of the day when I left Luka on the 27th of May until I was arrested on the 13th of July, I never left my flat. So it wasn't of much use to me. I did not really need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. H, can I ask you this: Apart from Dragisa Tesic, who you've described as a police inspector, was there also another police inspector whom you recognised at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kavrinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would that be Petar Kavrinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Petar, yes, Boro's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Like Mr. Tesic, had you known him before your detention at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. I knew his brother better, but I also knew him because he was also with the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you become aware, during your stay at Luka, that he was also interrogating detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: All sorts of rumours spread. Some were taken to Mr. Tesic, some were taken to Kole, the police chief or whatever he was called, of the camp. I don't know what they were called. Some were taken to Sasa's. So there were interrogations also at Mr. Tesic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would this be right: that these were the people who were taking decisions as to who should and who should not be issued passes, who should be detained, so on and so forth, who should be transferred; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: It is hard to say whether it is right or wrong. I should merely like to mention that -- I already said that Mr. Tesic had promised that nothing would happen to me, that no harm would come to me, and that I would be released after he consulted the gentleman, the above-mentioned Jelisic, and I guess, that's only my opinion, that some decisions must have been made there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Apart from saying that he wanted to speak with Mr. Jelisic about whether or not you should be released, was any further explanation of any kind given as to why he had to do that or why he wanted to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No, I don't know if he talked to Mr. Jelisic or not or whether he says that. I really cannot give you any definite answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as Mr. Jelisic is concerned, is this correct: that around the 15th or 16th of May, you believe that he left the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. And you know how I know that? That night, according to the chat among the soldiers, among the guards at Luka, they were to go, and as they put it, liberate a locality called Klanac. I believe that Jelisic turned up on the next day -- again I say I'm not sure about the date, whether it was the 15th or 16th -- with his hand bandaged. I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And that was the last that you saw of him whilst you were at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No. Jelisic was at Luka, but he came to our hangar very seldom because he had already had a man, and I've already mentioned him, Mr. Ozegovic, who did what he was supposed to do, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this right: that between the 16th of May and you seeing him or seeing him again at Batkovici, you did not see him between those two dates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I can't be quite certain if I saw him on the 16th and then not -- and any time between -- before the 27th because there were no crimes committed in the hangar, so we did not notice him. And because of that I really cannot tell you if he was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The reason I ask, Mr. H, and I want to just refresh your memory, is that you told the Office of the Prosecutor this: "Around the 15th, 16th of May, Vojkan, Goran, and a few more soldiers said, 'From today on there will be no more killings.'"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: "I believe it was that night that Goran left the camp. The next time I saw Goran was at Batkovici." Does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I just said that I could not really remember the date. As I said, we did not notice him -- we did not see him enter the hangar between that time we saw him with his hand bandaged and when we left. We did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. H, I want to ask you now very briefly about the three people you talked about earlier on: Novalija, Itric, and the painter. As far as the man Itric is concerned -- I'm sorry. Let me just deal quickly with the man called Novalija. As far as Novalija was concerned, is this right: Whatever his age, he was accused of being involved in being a sniper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And that that was the cause of the hostility towards him, was that he was suspected of having taken part in that activity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: These are assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it's an assumption or not, Mr. H, just answer the question. That was the focus of the hostility towards this man, the accusation that he was a sniper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As far as the man Itric is concerned, the focus of the hostility towards him was that he was alleged to have raped a young girl; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: By "young", I mean someone who is aged 7.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: That was said when Itric was brought into the hangar, that the child was 7 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. H, can you help me about this: In the country where I come from, people who are alleged to have raped small children are frequently treated with very considerable hostility, whether there's a war going on or not. Is that the case in your country? For example, when people are arrested, they have to be protected from the mob at a police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is moving outside the examination-in-chief. You're trying to get an opinion here out of the witness. Please move to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May I explain, please, Your Honour? If -- and I don't know whether this is the case in France or in Egypt, but it is certainly in England; it's something which does cause hostility. If he was killed because of that reason, it's not a reason that's connected with genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not accept the question. The question was asked in the examination-in-chief, and the witness answered that he thought that it was because Itric was allegedly suspected of having raped a young girl. What you can get from the witness now is only opinion and these are basically banal opinions. I think that raping a 7-year-old child, in every country of the world, is considered a very serious crime. It's not the witness saying that to you; it's the Judge. Please move to another question now. So you can think about that and limit yourself to what was part of the examination-in-chief, we're going to take a break, and I'll ask you to remain in the scope of the count of genocide and the scope of the examination-in-chief. Thank you. We're going to take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing will now resume. Have the accused brought in, please. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. H, I want to ask you now, please, about the man you describe as Alija. Is this right: that, in fact, his full name is Novalija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Novalija is his exact name and Smajlovic is his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the account you have given of this man Ohro. Would you accept, please, Mr. H, that today is the first time that you've ever mentioned the existence of this person when dealing with the matters concerning Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No, in view of the fact that in one of my statements I mentioned that man, and I don't know why it was not recorded in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And as far as the incident where you claim to have seen Mr. Jelisic with a TV crew at Batkovici, again, as far as the two statements that you made are concerned, you never mentioned that incident at all. So, again, today is the first time that you've mentioned that matter. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I think when I was giving my statement in Tuzla, this was quite some time ago, I don't know who the investigators were, and they were saying that they were not investigating the camp at Batkovici, and that is probably why this statement was not included.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to turn now, please, to the list of people that you've been through with the court and with the Prosecution. The first person on your list was somebody called Becirevic, otherwise known as Kibe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The information you have was that he was killed at the barracks sometime around the 11th of May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: These are stories, and I cannot give you the exact date when I heard this. At any rate, Kibe was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And help me about this, please. Is it within your knowledge that he was involved in politics in Brcko or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Sakib Becirevic, as far as I know, was not active. Mr. Hodzic was active, or Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can we please take them in turn, please, so we keep some order, mister --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was Mr. Becirevic -- did you know if he was a friend of Ibrahim Ramic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Butcher. Possibly. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like now to turn, if I may, please, to the second name that you mentioned, Midhat Bukvic. Your information was that he was killed at Luka. Do you know if he was involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No. Since his brother was a politician, I doubt he was a politician too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Stipo Glavocevic. You heard about his death. Can you tell us from whom you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: From the prisoners in Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think he was Croatian by ethnic background; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think he was a policeman at one stage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you know if he was involved in politics either before the war or during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I knew Stipo as a neighbour. We never had any other contact, so I didn't know anything about his political activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Sadik Jukic, which I think you'll find on the next page, Mr. H, a man in his 60s. You heard something about his death as having taken place in Mujkici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. In his basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: From whom did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: From my lady wife. At the time, she was in our house while I was imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And don't tell us your wife's name or anything, but did she hear it from somebody directly who knew exactly what had happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes, since he was not the only one who was killed. A woman was killed by Raymont, and he was too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you put a date on when you think he was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I left on the 13th of July. I went to Batkovici. Until the 5th of October, I didn't know a thing about my family either, and it was very hard. So I never even asked about this date of disappearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right. Do you know if Sadik Jukic was involved in politics before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: That's a man who's illiterate. He's a construction worker. He drove a vehicle with bricks, and concrete, and whatever. He had a family. I doubt he had any time to go into politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The next man, Mr. H, Jusuf Kapkovic, a man with a large family, disappeared on the 16th of June and has not been seen or heard of since. So apparently nobody can say what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No. No, there is no information about him, and he is listed as being missing, but nobody knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Again, Mr. H, do you know if he was involved in politics before his disappearance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Since he had a large family, and in view of his economic situation, I doubt it. This doesn't have to be correct, but I don't think he was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Next, please, two brothers, Katal, Hasim and Rasim, you think they were involved in sports. Would that be football?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes, played in Jadinsvo and in Lokomotiva [phoen], the local club in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And your information was that they were killed at Luka. From whom did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: From a gentleman I found in Luka who had been beaten up; Mr. Bukvic, that is, and it was probably conveyed to him from someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And he told us whilst he was still suffering from the effects of the beating, did he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Since Bukvic left Luka on the 14th or 15th, I think, there was time for us to have a chat every now and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The Katal brothers, were they involved in local politics? We have a description of them being involved as members of the local board.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: As for the political activity of the two of them, that, I don't know. I know they were sportsmen. I often went to Rasim's house. I don't know. As I said, I'm not aware of any political activity of these two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Then we turn next, please, and I think it's over the page, Mr. H, about halfway down that page, he was obviously an extremely well-known personality. You've described him as a very prominent citizen, and according to his son, he was taken from Janja. Is that a village or an area of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Janja is a very small town near Bijelina, perhaps 11 or 12 kilometres from Bijelina, with a population of about 13.000 now. He was there at the weekend cottage of a colleague of his. His son, who was detained in Batkovici together with us, said that they were taken together, but this man came to Batkovici, and where the other was taken, that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you describe him as a very prominent citizen, in what field? In what sphere was he prominent? What was the reason for his fame?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I think he was politically active. I don't know which party he belonged to, but that's why people knew him. I knew him because he was not far away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think there were three people called Pezerovic. Do you have those at the bottom of page 3, Mr. H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Are they all related, those three, or are two of them related and one not related?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: The first two, Ibrahim and Sevko, are brothers, and Suljo Pezerovic lived in Mujkici, in Bukovac [phoen]. I don't know whether they're related, but the first two are brothers, Ibrahim and Sevko.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the two brothers, did they live in Brcko or outside Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: They lived in Brcko, near the railway station and near the Lokomotiva football club stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Again, your information is that they disappeared and nothing is known of their fate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the same in the case of Suljo, who was known to have been arrested and taken away but has not been seen since?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: They are mentioned in the statement, I think. In relation to this Suljo, he was wounded somewhere. He was brought to Luka in blue pyjamas. You have it there in the statement. After the 15th or 16th, I don't know, he was taken away and he's never been seen since.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you know if any of the Pezerovics were involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Since Ibrahim Pezerovic is a manual labourer, he worked in a factory, and his brother was a railway station worker, he was a cleaner, I doubt that they were active anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Next, Senad Pobric. The only information you have about him is him disappearing in early May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Again, do you know if he was involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: That's a child, a young man, 25 or 26 at the time. He played football. I doubt he was interested in politics, but I don't know for sure. That is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: We have a date of birth of 1965, Mr. H, so he would have been in his late 20s in 1992. Would that be the person you know of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Franjo Vugrindzic [phoen], you list something as having happened to him. What did you hear about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I just heard that he was taken away. They lived at Maraja, behind the morgue of the hospital. He was taken away and he never returned. I think that his wife is of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. H. Could we now turn to the second of the two lists, Exhibit 13? I think you'll probably have that in front of you as well. It's just to your right-hand side there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: We forgot one person on this first page. Kombic, I think. Well, never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. On the first page of the -- what was the name you mentioned again? I'm sorry. Kombic. I do apologise. You're entirely right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Salik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The information you had about him was a disappearance but nothing further known?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, according to the information that we have or, rather, that I received, he disappeared together with Pobric, and there is another man who's not on the list. That was this new part of Brcko, Lozijono [phoen], whatever it was called. All of it is the same neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The second list, Mr. H. Ahmet Hodzic, better known as Papa --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: -- you were aware of him having been killed, but didn't know how. Would the description of him that's given here in English, "president of the local executive in Kolobara," would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I know that he was president of the local commune of Kolobara, but I don't know whether he was president of the local executive board as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. And a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: As I said, I do not know. I know that he was president of this local organisation, whatever it was called. I don't know whether he was a member. Possibly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Then the gentleman from whom you bought some land, Mr. Kaknjo, the same, he was someone who had made significant contributions to the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: According to the information that I have, I think he was politically active.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the description that we've got of him here, "important member of the board of the Islamic community," would that accord with your information about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: The Islamic community is not a political organisation. The Islamic community is an organisation which deals exclusively with Muslim affairs. It is not politically active.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Answer to the Judges, Witness H. You're answering the Judges. Thank you. Please proceed. Can we speed things up a little bit? Because I think you've gone longer than you said you would, but I would like you to finish under proper conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am drawing to a close, as Your Honour will understand as we go through this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. H, as far as the next name is concerned, Dr. Edhemovic, a very prominent man in the town; you would accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It describes him here as having no formal position in the SDA but an important associate of the party because of his influence in the town. Would that be a fair comment about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Vasif Sulejmanovic, a gentleman who owned the television station in Brcko. You've described him as wearing a white arm band. Do you know what the significance of a white arm band was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Next, the name of Zelenjakovic. You were aware of three brothers by that name; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were they involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Next, the name of Kevric, which I think you'll find on the final page at number 33. Again, known as a prominent citizen in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you believe that he and the next man named on the list were killed at the same time and the same place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: According to the persons from Srpska Varos, from that area, they were killed that night. I don't know. I know he worked at the railway station. I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As far as Mr. Muminovic is concerned, were you aware that his sons were involved in SDA politics and were members of the party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Finally, Osman Vatic, who you believe had given money to the SDA. Was he also an SDA member of parliament?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I never said that I believed he gave money. As we came into Luka, Mr. Jelisic said that he gave money. You do not have a statement of mine saying that I believed that he gave money, and I cannot say whether he was a member or not. He was a respectable citizen. Possibly he belonged to a political party too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I stand corrected about the information. Finally, Mr. H, I just want to go back briefly to the camp and ask you something I omitted to ask you earlier. Were you aware of someone working at the camp called Kole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this right: He was in command of the police unit at Luka throughout your time there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: During those 15 days, and that is how long I stayed there, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Tochilovsky, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: I do not have any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. H. We have to call you Witness H. Excuse me. Perhaps you can clarify just two points for me. I noticed first, and this is just a minor question, that when you mentioned that some people were killed or disappeared, you used several different descriptions. For some people, you would say that there is no trace of them; and for other people, you would say that they are no longer among the living; and for some people, you would say that they had been killed. I noticed some losses in what you said. Other people, you said, yes, they were killed, one was killed in front of his house; another was, I think, killed in the same hangar as you. This was very clear. But others, one of them, you said, "I heard that he was killed." That was also clear. But when you said that they were not among the living, what does this mean? How do you know? Does that mean that they disappeared and nobody knows where they are or that it has been proved that they are killed? Perhaps you can just clarify this, if you can. I can give you the names even.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No, I don't need names really. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: (redacted). On the basis of information, I believe that the names I mentioned when I said that all trace is lost, I mean I think I'm right. However, "killed," "missing," I think to our minds, it is the same. They are not among the living. They are no longer alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So this is now the general idea, that those who are missing, as you said, are not among the living.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: These are assumptions only, but I have never called, and the war ended in 1995, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And they are legally treated as not living any more? Legally, do you know that? Their wives can get married and that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, they are getting married, so this is not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Another more disturbing question: You mentioned that some people were being considered as snipers. Mr. Novalija Smajlovic, 70 years old, I think, or more, was called a sniper and was beaten to death. I think Mr. Muminovic was considered that he was financing the SDA and then treated accordingly. Mr. Stjepan Itric was accused of raping a 7-year-old girl and then beaten to death also, or at least what you said: is not any more among the living. Were these accusations just distributed on the people, each one being called something, as if when you call somebody Mr. John or Mr. Robert, or there was a legal inquiry and some kind of legal sentence, putting them to prison, sending them to prison, or even the death sentence? Was this some kind of legal process or just, at random, calling everybody whatever you like and then treating them accordingly? In your view, what was happening exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Let me tell you, there were no laws. People who were killed or who were brought in were interrogated very seldom. I already mentioned about Itric, that that same day, he was brought in and battered. I should like to mention something. You mentioned Mr. Muminovic, that he financed or that I said something to that effect. I did not quite get the question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I heard that Muminovic was accused of giving money to the SDA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was just an example, anyhow. Someone was giving money and was being punished for that. So these punishments were not based on any legal basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What were they based on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: It is really hard to say. I can say that I was brought from a hospital bed, with eight other patients from that same hospital, and they did not call any names; they simply said, "If you're a Bosniak, you are taken in." So that was the procedure, but it had nothing to do with law. It was not a lawful procedure; it was a physical procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Some were, as you mentioned, spared; and some were, as you said, did not survive. Was there some kind of selection, selecting somebody and then letting someone else get away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Anything is possible. They also had some connections or maybe some friends, and they survived, and I'm probably one of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm happy you are one of those. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Witness H, good afternoon. I also have a few questions to ask. When we speak about Mr. Itric, I think that you left your house on the 4th of May, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And Mr. Itric, do you know when it was that he left his house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I believe it was on the 13th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, you left your house before he did because you had to go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Before leaving your house to go to the hospital, (redacted) (redacted), in the community in your village, were there any accusations brought against Mr. Itric, accusations of his having raped a young girl?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No. He was a very quiet man. I did say in a statement that we never even saw him with a female, with a woman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Is it possible that that could happen after you left the hospital and his arrest, when he was taken to the Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I doubt it really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Then when at the Luka camp you heard that accusation, were there other neighbours of Mr. Itric there, there at the Luka camp? Excuse me. In the Luka camp, were there other individuals besides yourself who knew Mr. Itric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. There was his next-door neighbour, Suljo Hasimbasic. There was his father brought, I don't know on what date. I believe on the 18th is when he was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: When faced with this accusation, how did the people who knew Mr. Itric react?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: At that time, when he was brought in, Hasimbasic and his father were not there, because he had gone out to buy cigarettes for his father. So they couldn't react.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And you, how did you react?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: We were not allowed even to look. We all had to keep our heads down and look at the floor. There was -- no reaction would be called for, because I could have been also beaten or killed for reacting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But within yourself, do you think that the accusation was valid or not valid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Because I know the man, as I already explained, I think it is false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And the other accusation that you spoke about when you spoke about an old man who was 82 years old and who was accused of having been a sniper, was he in physical condition in order to go fight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: That is, was he in good health?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: He was a man who seemed to be in a very bad shape, and he also wore glasses. I do not think his sight was even all that good. Therefore, I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, there were many accusations against several people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: There is something else I would like to know. You recognised, on the two lists, at least 20 people, not counting the people whose name appears on both. Is there something in common among all of these people? Could one find any kind of common denominator for all those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: They're all people from different parts of the town. I doubt, or, rather, I should say that they have nothing in common.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I don't want to lead my questions. You recognised at least 20 people. Among the 20 people whom you recognised on both lists, did any of them have a common characteristic to all of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Could you construct any kind of sentence saying all of those people were something? Let me go further than that. Of what ethnic group were these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: They were all Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And what was their religion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Muslims. Excuse me, except for Stipo Glavocevic and Itric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. We know that they were Croats. You spoke about people who were arrested and then released on the same day. Do you remember that as those people who were arrested and released the same day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Who were they? Were they Muslims or were they members of another religion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I know only Zoran, who came from a mixed marriage. The priest, the orthodox priest in Brcko, came and took him away the same day. All the rest were Muslim or Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You spoke about the subject of your interrogation when you answered Mr. Greaves's questions. You mentioned a whole series of people about whom he wanted information. As regards those people you spoke about during your interrogations, were they also Muslims or were they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Those who interrogated or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The people who conducted the interrogation asked you information about certain people. You mentioned some of them in your answer to Mr. Greaves's questions. Who were those people who wanted to find out information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: They were mostly interested in people who were Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Another question. As regards the discussion around 11th -- or 13th of May, when you gave your answer to Mr. Greaves, you spoke about statements that were given to the Bosnian authorities, I believe. What type of authorities were they? Were they administrative, or military, or judicial authorities? What type of authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: In my first statement, it was given to administrative authorities; that is, a wartime journalist, Suad Alagic, I believe his name was, was the one who took my first statement. My second statement I gave to the investigators, and I believe it was in 1994, 1995. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: When you showed us your laissez passer, there were also authorities who issued it. Who were those authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I already said it. I was issued that pass in the office in which Mr. Korenovic and Mr. Tesic worked. Who signed that pass, I don't know, but they -- those were the authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But mention was made of the authorities. In the upper left-hand corner, you saw there were five lines. Which authorities were mentioned there? Were these also Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: No. Those were Serb authorities or, as far as I could read it out, it was the Serb public security station in the Serb Autonomous Province of Semberija. So those were the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But they were Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Something else with which I'll conclude. In your summary, you mention Kolar; that is, someone who went by the name of Kolar. When you answered Mr. Greaves about Mr. Kolar, were Kole and Kolar the same people or are they different people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Kolar, his surname is Smajlovic. We called him Kolar because he had a horse and a cart, and that is how he earned his livelihood, and Mr. Kole is a Serb, and they are not related in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So these are two different people. I thought that I -- that this was the first time today that you spoke about Kole, because Mr. Greaves mentioned the fact that you had never referred, in your previous statements, to him, that this was the first time that you mentioned Kole. Is that correct, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: Well, it was not in the statement, so I suppose I could not -- I could not have not mentioned him, because I knew Kole personally. I also knew his mother. Because of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness H, for interrupting you. Mr. Greaves, you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It was concerning the man Ohro, not Kole, that I suggested that he'd not mentioned him before, a man called Ohro, not Kole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, in any case, but I go back to my question. Why is it only today that you spoke for the first time about that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I just said so now. Invariably, in my statements, I spoke about Mr. Kole, because Mr. Kole was some kind of a police chief down there in Luka. I don't know how many people there were with regard to the police administration. I don't know what the reason was why he was not included in the record. That I don't know. Whether it was that unimportant or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Really my last question now. When you signed your statements to the Bosnian authorities, did those people give you the statements so you could read them and ask you whether you agreed before you signed, or how did things occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS H
utterances.text: I think it was the day after the day I was released from Batkovici. As I say, this statement was taken by a journalist and nothing was given to us to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness H. Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. President. Excuse me for having taken so much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the very complete nature of your nature, I can spare the witness my own questions because they were already answered. I will take advantage of this time -- I'll give you the floor, Mr. Tochilovsky. I would like the registrar to tell us whether there are any problems with the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statements of Witness H are reference numbered 28, 28A for the French version and 28B for the B/C/S version. And the laissez passer, which was presented, will have the number D7, and this is a confidential exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me turn to my colleagues and ask whether we can accept as an exhibit the statements made before the Tuzla authorities so that the Judges try to see if there is an overarching consistency in them. Mr. Tochilovsky?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: First of all, if the statement given to Bosnian authorities is accepted as an exhibit, we would like a statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor also to be admitted into evidence as an exhibit, but I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been very careful to put it to him in two ways: one to refresh his memory; and, two, alternatively to ask him not an inconsistency, but why he hadn't mentioned something before. That is not an exercise which requires Your Honour to see the statement, in my submission. The first point is simply to clarify with the witness whether he has perhaps mistaken the dates, and the second matter is perfectly simple. It's accepted he didn't say it and he's not -- he's given an explanation as to why he didn't mention it. So it doesn't require Your Honour to have the two statements to make any comparison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges maintain their decision because the coherence of various statements is really brought into question rather seriously, and you -- you have less pointed at these differences in the case of this witness, but the Judges also believe that there may be contradictions between the statements, and it is quite legitimate to ask them and the Judges, who will have to decide at some point about them. Yes, Mr. Tochilovsky, you have the floor. You have something to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Just one issue. The Defence mentioned to the witness, and then reiterated again, that the witness never mentioned the name "Ohro" in his previous statements, and I believe if this is the Defence position, it's not correct, because on page 7 of the statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor, there is a paragraph on Ohro where the witness says: "A detainee by the name 'Ohro' beat the detainees at Luka." It is on page 7 in the English translation. I believe it is also in French and in Bosnian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I accept that's what it says. Of course, he's given rather more information than simply that bland statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Before we adjourn for the day, I should like to ask the Prosecution for these lists. Were these lists established on the basis of all the testimonies, and thus you drew up these lists and tried to finalise them? Could you please explain how you did them? What was the procedure? I'm really sorry. Mr. Nice, it is you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The two lists are different lists entirely. One came from Bosnian authorities and is a document that a witness coming next week, the Chief of Prosecution, John Ralston, will deal with, and that purported to be a list dealing with bodies in mass graves, and giving an account --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other list, list 39, is a list produced by a witness, whom I shan't name at the moment, but is simply a list of prominent Muslims. So one is more directly identified as a list of those said to be dead, although the people saying they're dead are the Serbian authorities, contemporaneously giving an account of their death and some kind of explanation for their death, but nevertheless, giving an account of the bodies in the grave. The other is a list of prominent Muslims. They're different lists, but certainly we'll have the best available evidence of those lists, and each of them, from witnesses within the next week. I hope that helps. The Tribunal will remember that, of course, it was the Defence who indicated that they were going to ask questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- about these lists that led to my attempting to save time by asking them about the questions first. While I'm on my feet, and I know it's late, but may I simply mention, because it will help, two short administrative matters? Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not yet, but I should like to go into private session, if possible, before we proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 6.42 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of September, 1999, at 10.00 a.m.
